titulo: The Underworld and Saints of the Raval
intro: The Raval was once farmland, then a monastery, then Barcelona's densest and most notorious neighbourhood — the old "Barrio Chino" — and today it's a mix of contemporary art, immigration and thousand-year-old churches surviving right next to centuries-old bars. It's the least postcard-perfect face of Barcelona, and precisely for that reason, the most honest. It's about 2 km.
puntoPartida: Mercat de la Boqueria, main entrance from La Rambla

paradas.titulo: The circle painted by a neighbour
paradas.llegada: Standing at the Boqueria's entrance, look down: there's a large, colourful circular mosaic set into the pavement.
paradas.enigma: This mosaic was designed by an artist born just metres from here, on the now-vanished Passatge del Crèdit. It was installed in 1976. What was the painter's name?
pistas: He's one of the most famous 20th-century Catalan painters, alongside Dalí and Picasso.
His shapes are simple: circles, stars, primary colours.
The artist is Joan Miró.
paradas.historia: Miró chose this spot on purpose: he'd been born just steps away. The mosaic, 8 metres across, is made of coloured cement and crushed glass — the same kind of material Miró used in his public sculptures across the city.
paradas.fuente: Ajuntament de Barcelona; Fundació Joan Miró

paradas.llegada: Walk along Carrer Nou de la Rambla to the Palau Güell, the light-stone façade with two large entrance arches.
paradas.enigma: Gaudí designed this house for Eusebi Güell, between two enormous wrought-iron doors. Between the doors there's a lattice bearing the coat of arms of Catalonia, crowned by a helmet with a winged creature. What creature is it?
pistas: It's not the bat from the Arc de Triomf, though that's also a heraldic symbol.
It's the same mythical creature from the legend of Sant Jordi (Saint George).
It's a winged dragon.
paradas.historia: This façade dates from 1888, one of Gaudí's first major commissions, more than twenty years before the Sagrada Família. On the rooftop, invisible from here, there are twenty different chimneys and a bat-shaped weathervane — the same heraldic animal you've already seen if you've played the El Born route.

paradas.titulo: The hospital that now lends books
paradas.llegada: Walk to Carrer de l'Hospital and find the entrance to the courtyard of the Antic Hospital de la Santa Creu.
paradas.enigma: This Gothic hospital cared for the sick from its founding until it closed its doors in 1926. Look for a date carved somewhere in the courtyard or on an information panel: what year did the hospital begin operating?
pistas: It's a year in the early 15th century.
It's a little over 500 years before today.
The hospital opened in 1414.
paradas.historia: For centuries this was Barcelona's general hospital; today its buildings house the Biblioteca de Catalunya and the Massana art school. Every Corpus Christi, the courtyard fountain hosts "l'ou com balla": a hollow egg that literally dances on the water jet — a tradition that hasn't missed a year in centuries.
paradas.fuente: Biblioteca de Catalunya; Ajuntament de Barcelona

paradas.llegada: Walk to Sant Pau del Camp, the small stone church with a low, simple portico, the oldest in the Raval.
paradas.enigma: This is, by far, Barcelona's oldest church: a funerary stone from the year 911 helps date its origins, though the current building is mostly from the 11th century. Look closely at the entrance portico: the columns holding it up are a different style from the rest of the building. Where do those columns come from, according to historians? (one word: they are...)
pistas: Nobody carved them specifically for this church.
They come from earlier Roman or Visigothic buildings, much older than the church itself.
They're reused columns from earlier constructions.
paradas.historia: "Del Camp" means "of the fields": when it was built, this Benedictine monastery stood outside the city walls, surrounded by orchards. It survived an attack by Almanzor in the year 985 and centuries of history since — and it's still here, almost invisible, just steps from La Rambla.
paradas.fuente: Sant Pau del Camp; Generalitat de Catalunya, Patrimoni Cultural

paradas.titulo: The cat that couldn't find a home
paradas.llegada: Walk to the Rambla del Raval and find the large bronze cat sculpture, lying on a stone base.
paradas.enigma: This sculpture is the work of a Colombian artist famous for his rounded, voluminous figures. The city council bought it in 1987, but it took sixteen years to find it a permanent home here. What is the sculptor's name?
pistas: He's Colombian, and his figures — people, animals — are always plump and rounded.
His surname starts with B.
The sculptor is Fernando Botero.
paradas.historia: Before arriving here in 2003, the cat spent time in Parc de la Ciutadella and at the Olympic Stadium during the 1992 Games. Today it's one of Barcelona's most photographed — and most climbed-on — sculptures. Botero, they say, doesn't seem to mind.

paradas.titulo: The white cube of the skaters
paradas.llegada: Walk to Plaça dels Àngels and find the large white building with a rippled glass façade.
paradas.enigma: This contemporary art museum was designed by an American architect and opened in 1995. Its dark stone plaza has become, without anyone planning it, one of the most famous skateboarding spots in Europe. What colour is the building?
pistas: It contrasts sharply with the plaza's dark paving.
It's the colour of light, the absence of colour.
The building is white.
paradas.historia: The architect is Richard Meier, known for his white, luminous buildings. Nobody designed this plaza with skateboarding in mind, but its granite steps and benches turned out to be perfect for it — and today it's as famous among skaters worldwide as the museum itself is among art lovers.
paradas.fuente: MACBA — Museu d'Art Contemporani de Barcelona

paradas.titulo: The oldest bar in the city
paradas.llegada: Walk to the corner of Carrer de Sant Pau and Carrer de Sant Ramon, where you'll find Bar Marsella, with its early-19th-century decor.
paradas.enigma: This is Barcelona's oldest bar, famous for serving absinthe and for having Hemingway, Picasso and Dalí at its counter. Look for the founding year, usually visible on its façade or menu. What year did it open?
pistas: It's a year in the early 19th century, in its first two decades.
The bar has been open for over 200 years.
It opened in 1820.
paradas.historia: The worn mirrors, hanging lamps and marble tables are original to the period. The traditional way of serving absinthe here — with a small spoon, a sugar cube, and water dripped slowly over it — is still the same used when Picasso came looking for conversation and inspiration.
paradas.fuente: Bar Marsella; historical chronicles of the Raval

paradas.titulo: The cinema where something else used to be
paradas.llegada: Finish at Plaça de Salvador Seguí, home to the modern building of the Filmoteca de Catalunya.
paradas.enigma: This building, with its large glass façade, opened to give the Filmoteca a new home. Before this, this square and its streets were part of the old "Barrio Chino," Barcelona's red-light district for much of the 20th century. What year did the current building open?
pistas: It's a year from the 2010s, quite recent.
Fewer than 15 years separate that date from today.
It opened in 2012.
paradas.historia: The design is by architect Josep Lluís Mateo. That a temple of cinema and culture now occupies a square that for decades meant something else entirely sums up the Raval's recent history well: a neighbourhood that has reinvented itself several times without ever stopping being, deep down, the same — dense, mixed, and alive.

final.titulo: You've crossed the other historic centre
final.texto: From a mosaic by Miró to a wrought-iron dragon, from a hospital that now lends books instead of medicine to the city's oldest church, from a cat that took sixteen years to find a home to a bar that's served absinthe for two centuries. The Raval has never been Barcelona's prettiest neighbourhood — but it might just be its most alive.
